papers.title: How Far Can Linear Go? BiPert, a Unified Framework for Single-Cell Perturbation Modelling
papers.abstract: Understanding how genetic perturbations affect cellular behaviour is essential for studying gene function and regulatory mechanisms. Large-scale CRISPR screens measure these effects across thousands of genes, but cover relatively few cellular contexts. Predicting perturbation responses in unseen cell types and identifying perturbed genes from their transcriptional effects therefore remain challenging. Here, we show that both tasks can be addressed through a common linear decomposition of transcriptional responses into shared and perturbation-specific components. Building on this principle, we introduce BiPert, a simple linear framework for both forward perturbation prediction and inverse identification. For forward prediction, BiPert outperforms existing methods that use no external biological knowledge when predicting gene expression changes in unseen cell lines. Its few-shot extension, BiPert-FS, adapts to new cell lines using as few as ten measured perturbations. For inverse identification, BiPert-ID identifies perturbed genes from single-cell expression profiles, outperforming deep-learning methods in unseen cell lines and donors. We further show that perturbations whose effects transfer more consistently across cellular contexts are also easier to identify, even after controlling for perturbation effect size. Together, these results establish a connection between perturbation transfer and identification, and demonstrate that simple linear models provide strong, interpretable baselines for both tasks.

papers.title: Beyond the Blueprint: The Continuing Evolution of Turing's Theory of Morphogenesis
papers.abstract: Turing's article ``The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis'' has profoundly influenced conceptual views on the emergence of biological form across scales and species. It has also served as a foundational framework to guide experimental investigations into the mechanisms that underlie pattern formation. In this article, we trace the historical development of Turing's ideas and examine their integration into contemporary research programs. We critically assess the broad and often overlapping concepts that have derived from Turing's work, both highlighting value in productive applications of the theory and suggesting that skepticism should remain in overly simplistic validations. By clarifying these concepts and their intrinsic limitations, we rethink contemporary approaches aimed at understanding the essential principles that govern biological pattern formation. We pose some important challenges that will require interdisciplinary expertise to overcome, and which will necessitate fundamentally new paradigms to understand the physical origin of Darwin's ``endless forms most beautiful''.

papers.title: VCBench: Benchmarking virtual cell models for in-the-wild perturbation response
papers.abstract: Virtual cell (VC) models aim to predict cellular responses to diverse perturbations in silico, offering great promise for drug discovery and precision medicine. However, although models routinely report strong performance on existing benchmarks, whether these predictions translate to practical biological utility remains unclear. Current evaluations often rely on overly simplified or inconsistent setups that fail to capture the complexity and variability of real biological systems. Here, we present a standardized, modular benchmarking framework that evaluates nine VC models under challenging, in-the-wild scenarios spanning unseen cell lines and donors, novel genetic and chemical perturbations, and cross-study transfer. Across these evaluations, complex models do not consistently surpass simple linear baselines on broad transcriptional trends, while fine-grained, perturbation-specific effects remain difficult to recover. Moreover, different evaluation metrics emphasize distinct biological properties, resulting in markedly different model rankings. Consequently, model selection and data integration strategies should be tailored to specific downstream tasks rather than applied uniformly. Together, this framework establishes a more biologically grounded benchmark to guide model development, evaluation, and deployment in real-world settings.
